questions.title: What is the standard of review for a district court's dismissal of an indictment?
questions.question_body: In Section II, the Fifth Circuit states they review the sufficiency of an indictment de novo. I'm confused about how this standard interacts with the three requirements listed (enumerating elements, informing defendant, double jeopardy defense). Does de novo review mean the appellate court ignores the district court's reasoning entirely, or just the conclusion? How does this standard specifically apply when the district court dismisses based on a failure to state an offense rather than a lack of evidence?

questions.title: How does Ciminelli define 'traditional property interest' in the context of fraud statutes?
questions.question_body: The opinion relies heavily on Ciminelli v. United States to distinguish between economic information and property. Ciminelli held that the 'right to control' assets isn't a traditional property interest. I'm struggling to understand the boundary here. If the defendants deprived followers of valuable economic information (the right to know the true price), why isn't that a property interest under Ciminelli? What specific characteristic makes money or securities 'traditional property' while information is not?

questions.title: What distinguishes 'fraudulent-inducement' from the rejected 'right-to-control' theory?
questions.question_body: Section III.A explains that the indictment alleges a 'fraudulent-inducement theory' rather than a 'right-to-control theory.' The court says fraudulent-inducement is 'not a repackaging of the right-to-control theory.' Can someone clarify the legal distinction between these two theories? If both involve deception, why does one protect property (inducement) while the other only protects information (control), and why does that distinction matter for the sufficiency of the indictment?

questions.title: Does an intent to profit satisfy the 'intent to defraud' element under Kousisis?
questions.question_body: In Section III.B, the court cites Kousisis to reject the argument that defendants must intend to harm the victim. The opinion states that intending to profit is sufficient because the defendants 'had money in mind.' I'm confused about the mens rea here. If a defendant intends to make money without intending to hurt the victim's bottom line, how does that constitute an 'intent to defraud' rather than just aggressive trading? What is the specific mental state required under Kousisis?

questions.title: Is actual economic loss to the victim required for a securities fraud conviction?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that 'fraud statutes do not require a victim to suffer an economic loss from a defendant’s scheme' and mentions the rejection of a 'mirror image' requirement. If the followers bought securities at market value (even if artificially inflated), does the fact that they received the stock negate the fraud? How does Kousisis allow a conviction when the victim receives something of value in return for their money?

questions.title: Why does the Fifth Circuit borrow from mail and wire fraud precedents to interpret 18 U.S.C. § 1348?
questions.question_body: Section III notes there is 'scant caselaw construing the securities fraud statute in this circuit' and that § 1348 'borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes.' Is there a specific legislative history or statutory language that mandates this borrowing? Does this mean all elements of § 1348 are identical to §§ 1341 and 1343, or are there specific nuances in securities fraud that limit this analogy?
